\begin{proof}
A cubic over a field is irreducible if and only if it has no root in that field. The cubes in $\mathbb Z_7$ are
\[
0^3=0,\quad 1^3=2^3=4^3=1,\quad 3^3=5^3=6^3=6.
\]
Since $2$ is not a cube modulo $7$, $p(x)=x^3-2$ has no root in $\mathbb Z_7$. Since $-2=5$ is also not a cube modulo $7$, $q(x)=x^3+2=x^3-5$ has no root. Thus both polynomials are irreducible.

Define
\[
\tau:F[x]/(p)\longrightarrow F[x]/(q),\qquad \tau(f(x)+(p))=f(-x)+(q).
\]
This is well-defined because
\[
p(-x)=(-x)^3-2=-(x^3+2)=-q(x),
\]
so $(p(-x))=(q(x))$. The map is a ring homomorphism, with inverse given by the same substitution $x\mapsto -x$. Therefore the quotient fields are isomorphic:
\[
F[x]/(p(x))\cong F[x]/(q(x)).
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}
For a cubic polynomial over a field, irreducibility is equivalent to having no root in the field. The cubes in $F=\mathbb Z_7$ are $0,1,1,6,1,6,6$. Neither $2$ nor $5=-2$ occurs among these values. Hence neither $x^3-2$ nor $x^3+2=x^3-5$ has a root in $F$, so both $p$ and $q$ are irreducible.

Consider the substitution homomorphism $\sigma:F[x]\to F[x]$ defined by $\sigma(f(x))=f(-x)$. Since
\[
\sigma(p(x))=p(-x)=-x^3-2=-(x^3+2)=-q(x),
\]
we have $\sigma((p))=(q)$. Consequently, $\sigma$ induces a well-defined homomorphism
\[
\overline\sigma:F[x]/(p)\to F[x]/(q),\qquad f(x)+(p)\mapsto f(-x)+(q).
\]
Because $\sigma^2$ is the identity, $\overline\sigma$ is its own inverse. Thus it is an isomorphism, and
\[
F[x]/(p(x))\cong F[x]/(q(x)).
\]
\end{proof}

Let $F=\mathbb Z_7$. The cubes of elements of $F$ are $0,1,$ and $6$. Since $2$ and $-2=5$ are not cubes in $F$, the polynomials
\[
p(x)=x^3-2\qquad\text{and}\qquad q(x)=x^3+2=x^3-5
\]
have no roots in $F$. A degree-three polynomial over a field is reducible only if it has a linear factor, equivalently a root. Therefore both $p$ and $q$ are irreducible.

Define $\sigma:F[x]\to F[x]$ by $\sigma(f(x))=f(-x)$. We have
\[
\sigma(p)=p(-x)=-x^3-2=-(x^3+2)=-q.
\]
Thus $\sigma((p))=(q)$, and $\sigma$ induces a map
\[
\overline\sigma:F[x]/(p)\to F[x]/(q),
\qquad f+(p)\mapsto f(-x)+(q).
\]
This map is well-defined, additive, and multiplicative. Since applying $x\mapsto -x$ twice returns $x$, the induced map satisfies $\overline\sigma^2=\mathrm{id}$. Hence it is bijective and is a field isomorphism. Therefore
\[
F[x]/(p(x))\cong F[x]/(q(x)).
\]
\end{proof}
